tip: 'Enerzijds' pairs with 'anderzijds' for on one hand, on the other: 'enerzijds begrijp ik het, anderzijds vind ik het jammer'.
'Doordat' means because for an actual cause; use 'omdat' for a motive or reason: 'doordat de brug open was, kwamen wij te laat aan'.
The fixed phrase 'er een punt van maken om ... te' means to make a point of doing: 'om altijd beleefd te blijven'.
'Aangezien' means since or given that, a more formal way to say because: 'aangezien het al laat is'.
'Trouwen' takes 'met', so in Dutch you marry with someone: 'trouwen met zijn vriendin'.
'Weliswaar' pairs with 'maar' to mean admittedly X but Y: 'het is weliswaar koud, maar de zon schijnt'.
The phrase 'ergens achter komen' means to figure something out: 'zij is er nog niet achter' = she hasn't worked it out.
In a question 'zullen we...?' means 'shall we...?', a suggestion, not just the future: 'zullen we samen gaan' (shall we go together).
'Gaan' + infinitive marks a planned future: 'zij gaat komend voorjaar een marathon lopen' (she is going to run a marathon), signalling intention rather than a neutral prediction.
'Zou' plus 'moeten' plus infinitive gives advice, like 'should': 'hij zou meer moeten sporten' (he should exercise more).
'Zou willen dat' takes the past tense for a present wish: 'zij zou willen dat zij meer vrije tijd had' (she wishes she had more free time).
Fronting 'nauwelijks' (hardly) forces the verb before the subject: 'nauwelijks was hij vertrokken', not 'nauwelijks hij was'.
'Te' plus an adjective plus 'om ... te' means 'too ... to': 'te moe om ... te gaan' (too tired to go).
'Zowel ... als ...' means both ... and: 'zowel de leraar als de leerlingen' (both the teacher and the pupils).
'Ook al' means even though and puts the verb before the subject: 'ook al was iedereen moe' (even though everyone was tired).
'Hetzij ... hetzij ...' means either ... or: 'hetzij door studie, hetzij door ervaring' (whether by study or by experience).
A sentence-final 'hè' asks for agreement, like 'right?' or 'isn't it?': 'lekker weertje vandaag hè?' (nice weather today, right?).
When 'je' follows the verb, as after starting with 'zonder oefening', the verb drops its '-t': 'word je', not 'wordt je'.
After 'de eerste' (the first), 'om ... te' expresses the first to do something: 'de eerste om het probleem te signaleren'.
Separable verbs split around 'te': 'uitproberen' becomes 'uit te proberen', with the prefix left of 'te'.
'Ondanks' takes a noun, not a full clause: 'ondanks de vertraging' (despite the delay). For a clause use 'hoewel' or 'ondanks dat'.
Purpose wraps the infinitive in 'om ... te' meaning 'in order to': 'om te studeren' (in order to study), with 'te' just before the verb.
'Waardoor' = as a result of which, and it sends its verb to the clause end: 'waardoor zij het feest miste'.
'Dromen' pairs with fixed 'van', which becomes 'ervan' before 'om ... te': 'droomt ervan om ooit een boek te schrijven'.
'Tenzij' means unless; with its clause first, the main clause puts the verb before the subject: 'annuleren wij' (we cancel).
'Hoewel' means although and sends its verb to the end of the clause: 'hoewel het regende' (although it rained).
Front an adverb like 'desondanks' and the verb jumps ahead of the subject: 'desondanks bleef hij' (nevertheless remained he), not 'hij bleef'.
'Vergeten' can take a plain 'te' with no 'om': 'de deur op slot te doen' (to lock the door). Some other verbs add 'om te' instead.
'Klagen' takes 'over'. Before a 'dat' clause it becomes 'erover dat': 'hij klaagde erover dat de buren te veel lawaai maakten'.
'Geen kaas van gegeten hebben' is a fixed idiom meaning to have no clue about something: 'ze heeft er geen kaas van gegeten'.
